source_title: Humanitarian aid expected to enter Oleshky as localized Russia-Ukraine truce holds
source_excerpt:
Ukrainian officials slam strikes hurting civilians
A Russian drone strike ‌killed at least 14 people on a crowded rail platform in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro on Thursday, while five died in daytime strikes on two other provincial cities and a late-evening missile strike killed one person in the capital Kyiv, officials said.
The string of attacks jolted Ukrainian cities as a local truce in the southern region of Kherson raised cautious hopes for a resumption of diplomacy.
"Russia is deliberately hunting civilians: on trains, at stations, in residential buildings," Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said on the Telegram app.
"There is no justification for this terror, and there never can be."
A new missile attack hit districts of Kyiv just before 11 p.m. local time killing one person, the city's military administration said. Warehouses were set ablaze and falling debris ​damaged a building on the east side of the Dnipro River.
A few hours earlier, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had described the attacks ​as "very cruel" and "deliberate when everyone expects de-escalation steps."
Zelenskyy warned that Ukraine had intelligence "about ⁠preparations by the Russians of new ballistic missile strikes. We need the means ‌to take out all this Russian evil. We are expecting relevant decisions."
Russian military personnel pass by damaged vehicle on Thursday during a de-mining operation they conducted in the Russian-controlled Ukrainian town of Oleshky. (Russian Defence Ministry/Reuters)
The six-day truce brokered with U.S. help applied only to southern Ukraine's Kherson region, ⁠where a humanitarian mission was underway ⁠to provide relief to the Russian-held town of Oleshky, ‌marooned in a war zone since the start of Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion.
Both sides issued a virtually identical statement saying de-mining operations had ⁠been completed and the operation could begin to allow aid into the town and permit residents to head out if they wanted to leave.
Elsewhere, Russian drone and missile attacks on critical infrastructure, including the rail network, have upended civilian life and ravaged the economy. The strikes exploited an acute shortage of air defence missiles.
A site of the Russian jet drone strike in central Chernihiv, Ukraine, on Thursday. (Maksym Kishka/Reuters)
In Dnipro, state railway Ukrzaliznytsia ⁠said a jet-powered drone had struck a platform at the city's main station, where a commuter train was preparing to depart.
Mangled bodies lay scattered across the shrapnel-marked pavement, where patches of bright red blood had pooled up.
Police filled black body bags ‌amid the wail of an air-raid siren.
"And for what? What goal are they [Russians] trying to achieve?" said Svitlana Shcherbak, a 67-year-old traveller sheltering underground at the station. "I don't understand it at all."

Another attack on Dnipro hit a student dormitory, setting it ablaze, regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said. He added that a day of assaults had cut power ⁠to 350,000 households in the city.
Russia's mounting bombing campaign against Ukrainian cities has regularly killed civilians. Moscow has denied targeting civilians.
Two teenage girls ⁠were killed on a central street in Chernihiv in northern Ukraine, and three people died in strikes on residential buildings in the central city ⁠of Kremenchuk.
In Chernihiv, in addition to the two dead teenagers, 23 people — including four children — were wounded in a drone attack on a busy downtown street.
"Ordinary, peaceful people were attacked who were just going to work, going about their daily business, making plans for the day," said Dmytro Bryzhynskyi, head of the city's military administration.

In Kremenchuk, strikes on a residential block killed three people and wounded 32, the regional governor said.
Russian drones also ​struck city buses in three separate attacks on southeastern Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia, wounding six, officials there said.
Thursday's strikes came amid renewed efforts ​to revive U.S.-backed peace talks to ⁠end Europe's deadliest conflict since the Second World War.
New three-way talks are expected to take place this month, with Ukrainian officials including top presidential adviser Kyrylo Budanov urging new pressure on Moscow from Kyiv's partners.
